title: Poetry
tagline: Six famous couplets by Ghalib, Iqbal and Mir, and how a mushaira works.
canDo: You can recite, understand and applaud classic Urdu couplets

grammar.title: Poetic pronouns and verbs
grammar.body: Poetry keeps older forms: tujhe (to you, for tumhein), mere → mire/mere, jaane hai (for jaanta hai), pe (for par). They're still understood by everyone.

grammar.title: Izafat everywhere
grammar.body: dil-e-nadaan (foolish heart), dard-e-dil (pain of the heart), gham-e-ishq (the sorrow of love). The -e- links a noun to its describer or owner; poetry uses it constantly.

grammar.title: Two vocabularies
grammar.body: Everyday → poetic: phool → gul (flower), duniya → jahan (world), pyaar → ishq / mohabbat (love), aankh → chashm (eye), raat → shab (night). Knowing a few unlocks most ghazals and half of all film songs.

lessons.title: At the mushaira
lessons.blurb: Poetry in Urdu is a team sport. The audience has lines too.
lessons.canDo: You can follow, and join in with, the call and response of a poetry gathering

teach.title: How a mushaira works
teach.info: The poet says 'arz kiya hai'. The audience shouts 'irshad!'. The poet recites the first line, often twice. The audience repeats the best bit. Second line. Then everyone shouts 'wah wah!' and, if it was really good, 'mukarrar!' so the poet has to say it again.

teach.title: Reading a sher
teach.info: A sher is two lines that stand alone. The first sets something up; the second lands it. Poetic Urdu uses old pronouns (tujhe for tumhein), Persian links (dil-e-nadaan: heart-of-foolishness) and its own vocabulary.

teach.tip: nadaan = naive, foolish. He's talking to his own heart.
dard (pain) and dawa (medicine): Ghalib loved a matching pair.
dam nikalna = for the breath to leave: to die.
The poet's name in the last couplet is his signature. And yes, he's being cheeky about paradise.

options.text: Links the two words: ‘heart of foolishness’, a foolish heart
options.feedback: It's the izafat from Unit 14.
That's -o-, as in sher-o-shayari.
No. It's a link.

exercises.prompt: What is Ghalib saying in “dil ke khush rakhne ko Ghalib yeh khayal achha hai”?

options.text: Paradise is a comforting idea, whether or not it's true
options.feedback: Cheeky, and 150 years ahead of its time.
Read the first line again: he 'knows the truth' about it.
He's saying what it takes to keep it happy.

lessons.title: Iqbal
lessons.blurb: Allama Iqbal (1877–1938). Poet of ambition. Every Pakistani schoolchild knows these two.
lessons.canDo: You can recite and explain a couplet by Iqbal

teach.tip: jahan here is the plural 'worlds'. aur bhi = more, still others.
imtihan = exam, trial. Still the everyday word for a school exam.
buland = high, lofty. kar buland = make it lofty.
raza = will, what you consent to. The line that launched a thousand graduation speeches.

exercises.prompt: What's the message of “sitaron se aage jahan aur bhi hain”?

options.text: Don't stop here: there's always further to go
options.feedback: Aim past the stars.
He wrote it in the 1930s. It's a metaphor.

options.text: The stars are very far away
options.feedback: True, but he had a larger point.

exercises.explain: buland = high. Raise your khudi high.
Poetry has its own vocabulary, mostly from Persian.

The whole garden knows he's in love. The only one who doesn't is the rose: the beloved.

options.feedback: Everyone else can see it.
